claims.text: An MLIP trained on ab initio liquid-state data and combined with free-energy perturbation can substantially reduce the cost of calculating fusion and high-temperature free energies.
The proposed method can retain the entropy and anharmonicity fidelity needed for fusion-property calculations.
The proposed method will be cheaper than full ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD for elemental, binary, and possibly low-order multicomponent systems.
A reduced ab initio liquid-phase dataset is sufficient to train the proposed MLIP.
Free-energy perturbation can replace the full thermodynamic integration used in explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The intended temperature domain is approximately 10–20% below to 10–20% above the phase-transition temperature.
Previous elemental and binary studies have reported fusion free energies suitable for evaluating this method.
The MLIP can rapidly sample configurations while faithfully capturing vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Learning the potential-energy surface from a small, high-fidelity ab initio dataset enables accurate energy and force predictions at a fraction of the cost of full ab initio molecular dynamics.
Free-energy perturbation can iteratively correct residual free-energy discrepancies between the MLIP and explicit ab initio calculations.
The method will be at least one order of magnitude faster than ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The method will provide fidelity comparable to or better than TOR-TILD.
Phase free-energy errors can be kept below approximately 10%.
The primary validity domain is elemental and binary systems near melting.
Accuracy may deteriorate or become uncertain for highly multicomponent high-entropy systems because of their greater configurational complexity.
Transferability across relevant thermodynamic states and the required magnitude of perturbative corrections remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: The predicted speed claim specifies at least an order-of-magnitude improvement over ab initio MD, whereas the falsification rule requires an order-of-magnitude improvement over TOR-TILD. These are different baselines, so the stated prediction and decisive speed test are not aligned.
